extracted.intended_audience: EPA staff, state regulators and plan developers, reliability authorities (FERC/NERC/balancing authorities), industry stakeholders, tribal nations, environmental justice communities, and public policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic standards used in the EPA final rulemaking for existing and new electric generating units (EGUs), including benefit-cost monetization, environmental justice analysis, stakeholder outreach, and grid reliability considerations to inform state plan development and compliance mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: External peer review of technical report
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA initiated an external peer review panel to conduct a high-quality review of the technical report to ensure methodological updates are consistent with economic theory and reflect the latest science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers commended the draft update as an improvement and provided numerous recommendations for refining presentation and future modeling improvements, especially regarding climate change impacts and associated damages not currently included. Complete information about the external peer review, including the peer reviewer selection process, final report with individual recommendations, and EPA responses, is available on the EPA website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of updated SC-GHG estimates and technical documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An overview of methodological updates to SC-GHG estimates is provided in RIA section 4.2, with detailed explanation of each input and modeling process in the technical report 'EPA Report on the Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases: Estimates Incorporating Recent Scientific Advances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should rely on the technical report for inputs and modeling choices; supplemental materials (e.g., RIA and TSDs) provide more detail on endpoints, effect estimates, and valuation selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization and discounting of benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetized climate and health benefits are presented as projected present value (PV) and equivalent annual value (EAV) discounted to 2024 in 2019 dollars; climate benefits (SC-CO2) are discounted at 2 percent while health benefits are presented at 2, 3, and 7 percent discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIA provides PV and EAV estimates under different discount rates (e.g., climate benefits ~ $270 billion PV using SC-CO2 discounted at 2%). Analysts must recognize substantial uncertainties and limitations in monetizing benefits and that important benefits are not monetized; discussion of non-monetized benefits is in section 4 of the RIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of non-monetized effects and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The results present an incomplete overview; monetized estimates do not include important benefits the EPA is unable to fully monetize due to data and modeling limitations, and other health, welfare, and water quality benefits are not quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic conclusions should acknowledge omitted impacts and uncertainties; non-monetized effects are discussed qualitatively elsewhere (e.g., RIA section 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA definition of Environmental Justice (EJ)
rubrics_metrics.description: EJ is defined as 'the just treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of income, race, color, national origin, Tribal affiliation, or disability, in agency decision-making and other Federal activities that affect human health and the environment' so that people are fully protected from disproportionate adverse effects and have equitable access to a healthy environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to frame EJ analyses and stakeholder engagement in rulemaking and state plan development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of June 2016 Technical Guidance for Assessing Environmental Justice in Regulatory Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For regulatory impact analysis, EPA relies upon its June 2016 Technical Guidance, which encourages analysts to conduct the highest quality analysis feasible and states that a regulatory action may involve potential EJ concerns if it could create new disproportionate impacts, exacerbate existing disproportionate impacts, or present opportunities to address existing disproportionate impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should apply the Technical Guidance, recognizing data/time/resource constraints and tailoring analyses to media/circumstance. The Guidance frames three core EJ questions to be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three core EJ analytic questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of potential EJ concerns for regulatory actions should address: (1) Are there potential EJ concerns associated with environmental stressors affected by the regulatory action for population groups of concern in the baseline? (2) Are there potential EJ concerns associated with environmental stressors affected by the regulatory action for population groups of concern for the regulatory option(s) under consideration? (3) For the regulatory option(s) under consideration, are potential EJ concerns created or mitigated compared to the baseline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All EJ analyses in the rulemaking are organized to answer these three questions; different analytic methods inform different questions and should be interpreted accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of EJ analysis: proximity and exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA employs two types of analysis to address EJ questions: proximity analyses (baseline demographic proximity to affected facilities) and exposure analyses (air quality modeling-based future exposures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximity analyses can identify populations near sources but do not measure exposures or future impacts. Exposure analyses—based on future air quality modeling—can inform whether regulatory options create or mitigate EJ concerns (questions 2 and 3). Each analysis has unique limitations and uncertainties and should be considered independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity analysis criteria and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline demographic proximity analyses evaluate populations living near affected facilities (examples: within 5 km, 10 km, 50 km) to identify potential EJ populations of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results may show higher percentages of certain demographics near affected facilities (e.g., American Indian, below-poverty), but proximity does not capture variation in baseline exposures nor indicate exposures or impacts will occur. Methodology and results are provided in RIA section 6.4 and a technical report in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure analysis metrics, scope, and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure analyses are based on illustrative compliance scenarios and air quality modeling; pollutant metrics are limited to those used in the benefits assessment—ozone: maximum daily 8-hour average averaged across the April–September warm season (AS-MO3); PM2.5: annual average. Modeling uses state/fuel level emissions with facility-level baseline emissions at a resolution of 12 square kilometers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure analyses do not consider all potential impacts of meaningful engagement or some localized protections; results are relative to a projected baseline (subject to baseline uncertainty) and may smooth daily ozone gradients. Analysts should note metric limitations, spatial resolution, and scenario assumptions when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure analysis outputs: aggregated and distributional formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure analysis results are provided in aggregated form (national and state level overviews) and distributional form (detailed information about concentration changes experienced by everyone within each population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregated results for broad overviews and distributional results to examine detailed exposure changes across populations and demographic groups. Do not directly compare proximity and exposure analyses because they address different aspects of EJ questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance for small magnitude exposure changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because modeled ozone and PM2.5 concentration changes due to the rule are small relative to baseline concentrations and disparities, the rules are expected to have a small impact on the distribution of exposures across demographic groups; post-policy burdens are likely to remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should not infer substantial mitigation or exacerbation of disparities from small modeled changes. The rule may show modest widespread reductions with some limited areas experiencing small ozone increases; specific slight exacerbations/mitigations for certain groups may occur in particular years and states and should be interpreted with caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outreach and public engagement expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA conducted extensive outreach including opening a public docket for pre-proposal input, national community and tribal outreach calls, targeted webinars for tribal environmental professionals and EJ communities, and virtual public hearings to gather diverse viewpoints and provide information on effective engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should include multiple outreach channels and targeted engagement to affected communities, especially tribal nations and EJ populations, to solicit input and improve transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful engagement requirement for state plans
rubrics_metrics.description: States are required to conduct meaningful engagement with pertinent stakeholders as part of the state plan development process (revisions to subpart Ba implementing regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA underscores the importance of meaningful engagement; section X.E.1.b.i of the preamble provides more detailed information. Meaningful engagement is a required element of state plan development and should be used to inform plan design and identify potential localized impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: State consultation with reliability authorities and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: States are strongly encouraged to consult with relevant balancing authorities and reliability coordinators for affected sources and to share unit-specific requirements and compliance information in a timely fashion to promote early and informed reliability planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should demonstrate consultation in state plans. Strong system-planning processes that recognize roles of states, balancing authorities, transmission planners, and reliability coordinators help identify potential resource adequacy or reliability issues early and allow plan revisions when issues arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance flexibilities available to states
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA offers a suite of voluntary compliance flexibilities for states: clarifying circumstances to use RULOF for source-specific standards and compliance schedules; allowing emission averaging, trading, and unit-specific mass-based compliance mechanisms for certain subcategories provided they achieve equivalent emission reductions and, for some mechanisms, include a backstop emission rate; and offering compliance date extensions for unanticipated control technology delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may use these flexibilities to address reliability concerns if equivalent emission outcomes are achieved and required safeguards (e.g., backstop rates) are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term reliability mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A short-term reliability mechanism is available for new and existing units to provide additional flexibility through an alternative compliance strategy during acute system emergencies that threaten reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may elect to include this mechanism in their state plans to make it available to sources without needing DOE action under section 202(c). Section 202(c) remains available for emergency situations not covered by EPA's mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability assurance mechanism and approval criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A reliability assurance mechanism is available for existing units that intend to cease operating but, for unforeseen reasons, need to temporarily remain online to support reliability beyond the planned cease operation date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of this mechanism requires a specific and adequate showing of reliability need satisfactory to the EPA, is limited to the time substantiated (may not exceed 1 year), and EPA intends to consult with FERC for needs exceeding 6 months. These instruments will be presumptively approvable if they meet the requirements defined in the emission guidelines and are incorporated into state plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of resource adequacy and sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated resource adequacy implications via a final technical support document (Resource Adequacy Analysis) and conducted capacity expansion modeling and sensitivity analyses (e.g., higher electricity demand scenarios) to examine pathways for compliance that respect NERC reliability considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should review technical memoranda in the docket (e.g., IPM Sensitivity Runs, Resource Adequacy Analysis) when assessing reliability implications. Results indicate available industry pathways to comply without violating reliability constraints, but state-level planning remains critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of DOE section 202(c) as an emergency reliability mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE has authority under section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to order temporary generation (e.g., for 90 days, extendable in 90-day increments) to address emergency generation shortfalls; generation operating pursuant to such an order is deemed not to be operating in violation of environmental requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 202(c) is a primary federal mechanism to ensure generation is available in emergencies; EPA's short-term reliability mechanism supplements but does not replace 202(c). Historical use (e.g., CAISO and PJM in 2022) demonstrates applicability for short-term reliability needs.
